lines: A plant operations stakeholder asks for real time dashboards, covering every single plant.
Engineering goes ahead and ships exactly that, at genuinely real time freshness.
The cost of doing so quietly consumes the entire quarter's own infrastructure budget. The request was fulfilled to the letter, and engineering still ends up taking the blame for it.
So what actually went wrong here.
And what single document, written before the build ever started, would have genuinely prevented this.
answer: Nobody ever priced real time against any of its alternatives, and nobody wrote down who actually owns it if it breaks.
A proper data contract, with clearly priced tiers, would have forced exactly that conversation first, long before the build itself even began.

lines: Here's what a data contract actually is.
It's an upfront, written set of guarantees that a producer makes to a consumer, covering a dataset's own shape and its freshness.
It is never just a verbal promise, and never something either side quietly assumes on their own.
Real time, it turns out, is not really one single option on its own.
It sits right at the very top of an entire pricing curve.

That same dashboard request becomes three separate, concretely priced tiers instead. A fast, expensive one. A medium one. A slow, cheap one. Each one is a real choice a consumer can genuinely make with their eyes wide open.
Stating plainly what a given tier does not promise turns out to matter just as much as stating what it does promise.
That is exactly the gap a contract listing only its own guarantees always quietly leaves wide open.
A quarterly error budget, jointly defined by both sides together against one clearly stated target, changes everything.
It turns the question of just how unreliable this is allowed to be from an ongoing political argument into one single, agreed upon number both sides can simply check.
An error budget like that only actually works if spending it down is somebody's own specific, clearly named responsibility.
The contract itself names an owner for that breach well before it ever happens, never during the incident itself.
Pulling this together now.
A real data contract is written guarantees, genuinely priced tiers, a clearly stated non goal, a jointly agreed error budget, and a named owner for the day it eventually breaks.
None of those five pieces is actually optional.
A stakeholder is offered three separate, clearly priced tiers, and simply picks the fastest one, without ever reading its non goals or asking who actually owns a breach.
So what's genuinely still missing from this entire negotiation.
answer: Picking a price is not actually the same thing as agreeing to a contract.
Until the non goals and the breach's own named owner are also agreed to, that stakeholder has really only priced the request. They haven't actually accepted its full terms yet.
